claim: Centrioles organise centrosomes and template cilia and flagella.
source: Centrioles organise centrosomes and template cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about centriole function.

claim: Several centriole and centrosome proteins have been linked to microcephaly (MCPH), a neuro-developmental disease associated with small brain size.
source: Several centriole and centrosome proteins have been linked to microcephaly (MCPH), a neuro-developmental disease associated with small brain size.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the study.

claim: CPAP (MCPH6) and STIL (MCPH7) are required for centriole assembly.
source: CPAP (MCPH6) and STIL (MCPH7) are required for centriole assembly, but it is unclear how mutations in them lead to microcephaly.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the introduction and supported by prior research.

claim: The TCP domain of CPAP constitutes a novel proline recognition domain.
source: We show that the TCP domain of CPAP constitutes a novel proline recognition domain that forms a 1:1 complex with a short, highly conserved target motif in STIL.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TCP domain of CPAP forms a 1:1 complex with a short, highly conserved target motif in STIL.
source: We show that the TCP domain of CPAP constitutes a novel proline recognition domain that forms a 1:1 complex with a short, highly conserved target motif in STIL.
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements showing stoichiometry and crystal structures.

claim: Crystal structures of the CPAP-STIL complex reveal an unusual, all-β structure adopted by the TCP domain.
source: Crystal structures of this complex reveal an unusual, all-β structure adopted by the TCP domain and explain how a microcephaly mutation in CPAP compromises complex formation.
evidence: This is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A microcephaly mutation in CPAP (E1235V) compromises complex formation with STIL.
source: Crystal structures of this complex reveal an unusual, all-β structure adopted by the TCP domain and explain how a microcephaly mutation in CPAP compromises complex formation.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data showing reduced binding affinity and structural analysis.

claim: Complex formation between CPAP and STIL is essential for centriole duplication in vivo.
source: Through point mutations, we demonstrate that complex formation is essential for centriole duplication in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through functional rescue experiments in Drosophila.

claim: The CPAP–STIL interaction constitutes a conserved key step in centriole biogenesis.
source: Our studies provide the first structural insight into how the malfunction of centriole proteins results in human disease and also reveal that the CPAP–STIL interaction constitutes a conserved key step in centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by structural conservation between zebrafish and Drosophila and functional data.

claim: All eight identified MCPH genes encode proteins that localise to centrioles and/or centrosomes/spindle poles.
source: All eight identified MCPH genes encode proteins that localise to centrioles and/or centrosomes/spindle poles (Thornton and Woods, 2009; Hussain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in CPAP (DSas-4 in Drosophila) and STIL (Ana2 in Drosophila) in flies lead to defects in the asymmetric division of larval neural stem/progenitor cells.
source: In support of this possibility, mutations in the centriolar components CPAP (DSas-4 in Drosophila, here called dCPAP) and STIL (Ana2 in Drosophila, here called dSTIL) in flies lead to defects in the asymmetric division of larval neural stem/progenitor cells (Basto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in MCPH proteins in mice lead to complex phenotypes that can include, but are not restricted to, microcephaly.
source: Mutations in MCPH proteins in mice, however, lead to complex phenotypes that can include, but are not restricted to, microcephaly (McIntyre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The conserved proline-rich region (CR2) in STIL is within residues 231–619 of human STIL.
source: Yeast-two-hybrid experiments suggested that a region of human CPAP comprising its conserved C-terminal TCP domain (or G-box) can interact with a ∼400 amino acid (aa) region (residues 231–619) of human STIL (Tang et al., 2011). To try to identify the region of STIL most likely to be involved in an interaction with CPAP, we carried out a sequence alignment with multiple metazoan STIL proteins (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This analysis revealed a short (∼40 aa) highly conserved proline-rich region (CR2) (Figure 1A) within this interval.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and prior yeast-two-hybrid data.

claim: The TCP domain of D. rerio CPAP binds to D. rerio STIL fragment (residues 404–448) with a KD of approximately 2 μM.
source: To test whether this region of STIL could bind to the CPAP TCP domain, we recombinantly produced the TCP domain of Danio rerio CPAP and used isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) to test its ability to bind to a fragment of D. rerio STIL that spanned CR2 (residues 404–448) (Figure 1D, Table 1). The two proteins formed a 1:1 complex with a KD of ∼2 μM.
evidence: This is directly measured by ITC experiments.

claim: The N-terminal region of D. rerio STIL CR2 (residues 411–428) binds to the CPAP TCP domain with a KD of approximately 4 μM.
source: Next, we further split the peptide to test the binding contribution from its N-terminal (residues 411–428) and C-terminal region (residues 429–448). The N-terminal region exhibited an only slightly weaker binding (KD ∼4 μM) to the TCP domain, whereas the C-terminal region showed a very weak binding (KD > 500 μM) (Figure 1D; Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by ITC experiments.

claim: The C-terminal region of D. rerio STIL CR2 (residues 429–448) binds to the CPAP TCP domain with a KD greater than 500 μM.
source: Next, we further split the peptide to test the binding contribution from its N-terminal (residues 411–428) and C-terminal region (residues 429–448). The N-terminal region exhibited an only slightly weaker binding (KD ∼4 μM) to the TCP domain, whereas the C-terminal region showed a very weak binding (KD > 500 μM) (Figure 1D; Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by ITC experiments.

claim: The majority of the binding affinity between CPAP and STIL comes from interactions with residues within the first proline-rich region in CR2.
source: We conclude that the CPAP TCP domain binds to a short conserved motif in STIL (CR2) with a potentially biologically significant affinity, and that the majority of the binding affinity comes from interactions with residues within the first proline-rich region in CR2.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data comparing N-terminal and C-terminal fragments.

claim: The TCP domain of CPAP folds into a single layer β-sheet comprising approximately 20 consecutive antiparallel strands.
source: The TCP domain folds into a single layer β-sheet comprising ∼20 consecutive antiparallel strands connected by type I β-turns and is stabilised by an extensive hydrogen-bonding network.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The TCP domain β-sheet shows a twist of approximately 13 degrees.
source: The resulting sheet shows a twist of approximately 13° (i.e., the angle between the consecutive, hydrogen-bonded strands), slightly lower than the average value of 20° observed for typical β-sheets (Chothia, 1973; Murzin, 1992).
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure and compared to literature values.

claim: The TCP domain is predominantly monomeric in solution.
source: Crystal packing interactions involve only small protein interfaces, suggesting that the protein is biologically active as a monomer. Indeed both small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and size-exclusion chromatography—multi angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) experiments demonstrate that the TCP domain is predominantly monomeric in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by SAXS and SEC-MALS data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The STIL peptide binds in a polyproline II helical conformation along one edge of the TCP domain β-sheet.
source: The structure of the CPAP–STIL complex revealed that the STIL peptide binds in a polyproline II helical conformation along one edge of the TCP domain β-sheet.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: Three STIL prolines (P417, P421, and P423) pack against aromatic CPAP residues (F978, Y996, and F1015).
source: The STIL peptide binds to CPAP by four main mechanisms (Figure 1C). First, three STIL prolines (P417, P421, and P423) pack against aromatic CPAP residues (F978, Y996, and F1015) in a way that resembles target motif recognition by other described proline-rich motif (PRM) binding domains (Kay et al., 2000).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: STIL R418 makes a cation-π interaction with the phenyl ring of CPAP Y994.
source: Second, R418 (STIL) makes a cation-π interaction with the phenyl ring of Y994 (CPAP).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: STIL R418 is involved in a water-mediated hydrogen bonding network that includes CPAP residues H1003 and T1005.
source: Third, STIL R418 is further involved in a water-mediated hydrogen bonding network that includes CPAP residues H1003 and T1005.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Sidechain–mainchain interactions are formed between CPAP residues Y994, Q1019, and E1021 and the bound STIL peptide.
source: Finally, sidechain–mainchain interactions are formed between CPAP residues Y994, Q1019, and E1021 and the bound STIL peptide.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The CPAP and STIL residues involved in the interaction are highly conserved across metazoans.
source: The CPAP and STIL residues involved in this interaction are highly conserved across metazoans (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by conservation analysis in the figures.

claim: The structure of the wild-type and the E1021V mutant TCP domain are virtually identical (RMSD = 0.1 Å over 142 Cα pairs).
source: To test whether this mutation disrupts the organisation of the TCP domain, we obtained the crystal structure of D. rerio CPAP937–1124 carrying the E1021V mutation (Figure 1F; Table 2). The structure of the wild-type and the mutant TCP domain were virtually identical (RMSD = 0.1 Å over 142 Cα pairs) demonstrating that the TCP domain structure was not compromised.
evidence: This is measured from comparing the two crystal structures.

claim: The E1021V mutation in D. rerio CPAP decreases binding strength to STIL by approximately eightfold.
source: ITC experiments with WT D. rerio STIL404–448 showed that the mutation of residues F978, Y994, and F1015 decreased the binding strength by ∼20 to 40-fold (Figure 2A, left; Table 4), while mutation of E1021 decreased the binding strength by approximately eightfold.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments.

claim: Mutation of CPAP residues F978, Y994, and F1015 to valine decreases binding strength to STIL by approximately 20 to 40-fold.
source: ITC experiments with WT D. rerio STIL404–448 showed that the mutation of residues F978, Y994, and F1015 decreased the binding strength by ∼20 to 40-fold (Figure 2A, left; Table 4), while mutation of E1021 decreased the binding strength by approximately eightfold.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments.

claim: Mutation of CPAP T986 does not detectably perturb binding to STIL.
source: In contrast, mutation of T986, which is not predicted to be in the interaction interface, did not detectably perturb binding.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments and serves as a negative control.

claim: Alanine substitution of STIL P417, R418 or P421 decreases binding strength to CPAP by approximately 10 to 20-fold.
source: We also purified mutant forms of the D. rerio STIL404–448 peptide and tested their ability to interact with the WT D. rerio TCP domain in ITC experiments (Figure 2A, right, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Table 4). Alanine substitution of P417, R418 or P421 decreased the binding strength by ∼10 to 20-fold and alanine substitution of P423 by approximately twofold to threefold.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments.

claim: Alanine substitution of STIL P423 decreases binding strength to CPAP by approximately twofold to threefold.
source: Alanine substitution of P417, R418 or P421 decreased the binding strength by ∼10 to 20-fold and alanine substitution of P423 by approximately twofold to threefold.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments.

claim: Mutation of STIL residue N422 does not compromise binding to CPAP.
source: In contrast, the mutation of residue N422, which is not predicted to be in the interaction interface, did not compromise binding.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments and serves as a negative control.

claim: The dSTIL–dCPAP interaction interface is highly similar to the D. rerio complex (average pairwise RMSD of 1.2 ± 0.2 Å across an average of 118 ± 4 Cα pairs).
source: To confirm this, we solved the crystal structure of the TCP domain from Drosophila melanogaster DSas-4 (dCPAP) (residues 700–901) in complex with the region of Ana2 (dSTIL) equivalent to CR2 (residues 1–47) (Table 2, Table 5, Table 6; Figure 2C). The dSTIL–dCPAP interaction interface in this structure was highly similar to the D. rerio complex (inter-species alignments of the structures yielded an average pairwise RMSD of 1.2 ± 0.2 Å across an average of 118 ± 4 Cα pairs).
evidence: This is measured from structural alignment of the crystal structures.

claim: A consensus CPAP binding motif in metazoan STIL proteins is PRxxPxP.
source: Together, these data allow us to determine a consensus CPAP binding motif in metazoan STIL proteins (PRxxPxP, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and suggest that the described CPAP–STIL interaction constitutes a highly conserved step in centriole biogenesis.
evidence: This is derived from sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: Wild-type dSTIL-GFP rescues the unc phenotype of the dSTIL mutant.
source: Both proteins were expressed at similar levels and localised strongly to centrosomes in the presence of endogenous dSTIL (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Only the wild-type version, however, was able to rescue the unc phenotype and the centriole loss phenotype of the dSTIL mutant (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional rescue experiments in Drosophila.

claim: dSTIL lacking the first 45 amino acids (including the PRxxPxP motif) fails to rescue the unc phenotype of the dSTIL mutant.
source: We first expressed a version of dSTIL that lacks the first 45 aa (including the PRxxPxP motif required for the interaction with dCPAP). GFP-tagged wild-type dSTIL (dSTIL_WT-GFP) served as a control. Both proteins were expressed at similar levels and localised strongly to centrosomes in the presence of endogenous dSTIL (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Only the wild-type version, however, was able to rescue the unc phenotype and the centriole loss phenotype of the dSTIL mutant (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional rescue experiments in Drosophila.

claim: The dSTIL P11A:R12A double mutant fails to rescue the unc phenotype of the dSTIL mutation.
source: All three constructs strongly localised to centrosomes in the presence of endogenous dSTIL (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Both single mutants rescued the unc phenotype of the dSTIL mutation while the double mutant failed to do so (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional rescue experiments in Drosophila.

claim: The dSTIL single mutants P11A and R12A partially rescue the centriole loss phenotype.
source: The single mutants P11A and R12A were also able to partially rescue the centriole loss phenotype, whereas the double mutant P11A:R12A showed only a poor rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: The dSTIL P11A:R12A double mutant shows only a poor rescue of the centriole loss phenotype.
source: The single mutants P11A and R12A were also able to partially rescue the centriole loss phenotype, whereas the double mutant P11A:R12A showed only a poor rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: The interaction between dCPAP and dSTIL is essential for dSTIL function in centriole assembly.
source: These data strongly suggest that the interaction with dCPAP is essential for dSTIL function in centriole assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with mutant constructs.

claim: Wild-type dCPAP-GFP rescues both the unc phenotype and the centriole loss phenotype.
source: Wild-type dCPAP-GFP localised strongly to centrosomes and rescued both the unc phenotype and the centriole loss phenotype (Figure 3G,N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by functional rescue experiments in Drosophila.

claim: dCPAP_ΔC-GFP fails to rescue the centriole loss phenotype.
source: Strikingly, the rescuing ability of the mutant constructs strongly correlated with the predicted strength of dSTIL binding. dCPAP_ΔC-GFP failed to rescue, dCPAP-MC1 and dCPAP-MC2 rescued poorly, the MCPH mutation E792V showed an intermediate phenotype, while dCPAP-MC3 exhibited a robust rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: dCPAP-MC1 and dCPAP-MC2 rescue the centriole loss phenotype poorly.
source: Strikingly, the rescuing ability of the mutant constructs strongly correlated with the predicted strength of dSTIL binding. dCPAP_ΔC-GFP failed to rescue, dCPAP-MC1 and dCPAP-MC2 rescued poorly, the MCPH mutation E792V showed an intermediate phenotype, while dCPAP-MC3 exhibited a robust rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: The dCPAP MCPH mutation E792V shows an intermediate rescue phenotype.
source: Strikingly, the rescuing ability of the mutant constructs strongly correlated with the predicted strength of dSTIL binding. dCPAP_ΔC-GFP failed to rescue, dCPAP-MC1 and dCPAP-MC2 rescued poorly, the MCPH mutation E792V showed an intermediate phenotype, while dCPAP-MC3 exhibited a robust rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: dCPAP-MC3 exhibits a robust rescue of the centriole loss phenotype.
source: Strikingly, the rescuing ability of the mutant constructs strongly correlated with the predicted strength of dSTIL binding. dCPAP_ΔC-GFP failed to rescue, dCPAP-MC1 and dCPAP-MC2 rescued poorly, the MCPH mutation E792V showed an intermediate phenotype, while dCPAP-MC3 exhibited a robust rescue (Figure 3N; Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of centrosome numbers in larval brain cells.

claim: Low total levels of dCPAP at centrosomes might be sufficient for centriole duplication, as long as some interaction with dSTIL is maintained.
source: Together, these data suggest that the interaction between dCPAP and dSTIL is a key step in centriole assembly and is essential for centriole duplication. Furthermore, they indicate that low total levels of dCPAP at centrosomes might be sufficient for centriole duplication, as long as some interaction with dSTIL is maintained.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MC3 rescues well despite weak localization.

claim: The SAS-4 TCP domain is required for SAS-4 to accumulate at centrioles.
source: While SAS-4WT::GFP targeted to centrioles in the absence of the endogenous protein, SAS-4ΔTCP::GFP did not, and instead exhibited a diffuse accumulation in the pericentriolar material (Figure 4B). Thus, the SAS-4 TCP domain is required for SAS-4 to accumulate at centrioles and become incorporated into the microtubule-containing outer centriole wall.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in C. elegans.

claim: The SAS-4 TCP domain is required for SAS-4 to become incorporated into the microtubule-containing outer centriole wall.
source: While SAS-4WT::GFP targeted to centrioles in the absence of the endogenous protein, SAS-4ΔTCP::GFP did not, and instead exhibited a diffuse accumulation in the pericentriolar material (Figure 4B). Thus, the SAS-4 TCP domain is required for SAS-4 to accumulate at centrioles and become incorporated into the microtubule-containing outer centriole wall.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in C. elegans.

claim: Full-length SAS-4 interacts specifically with the N-terminal domain (aa 1–202) of SAS-5.
source: To determine if the failure of SAS-4ΔTCP::GFP to become incorporated in the centriole outer wall could be due to an inability to interact with SAS-5, we performed a pull-down assay to determine whether 35S-labelled in vitro translated SAS-4 fragments could interact with the N-terminal or C-terminal regions of SAS-5 bound to beads (Figure 4D). In vitro translated full-length SAS-4 interacted specifically with the N-terminal domain (aa 1–202) of SAS-5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neither the SAS-4 N-terminal nor C-terminal region (which includes the TCP domain) alone can be pulled down by SAS-5.
source: Interestingly, we could not further narrow down the region of SAS-4 required for this interaction. Neither the SAS-4 N-terminal nor C-terminal region (which includes the TCP domain) alone could be pulled down by SAS-5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments.

claim: The TCP domain is required but not sufficient for SAS-4 to interact with SAS-5.
source: This result suggests that although the TCP domain is required for SAS-4 to interact with SAS-5, it is not sufficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the pull-down experiments showing that neither fragment alone binds.

claim: A TCP domain-dependent interaction between SAS-4/CPAP and SAS-5/STIL is conserved and essential for centriole duplication in C. elegans.
source: Together, these data suggest that a TCP domain-dependent interaction between SAS-4/CPAP and SAS-5/STIL is conserved and essential for centriole duplication in C. elegans, but that the precise interaction interface may have diverged.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional and biochemical data in C. elegans.

claim: The precise interaction interface between SAS-4 and SAS-5 may have diverged from other metazoans.
source: Together, these data suggest that a TCP domain-dependent interaction between SAS-4/CPAP and SAS-5/STIL is conserved and essential for centriole duplication in C. elegans, but that the precise interaction interface may have diverged.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to identify a PRxxPxP motif in worm SAS-5 and the requirement for both N- and C-terminal regions of SAS-4 for binding.

claim: The TCP domain structure represents an unusual, novel architecture.
source: The structure of the TCP domain represents an unusual, novel architecture.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison to known protein structures.

claim: The TCP domain structure lacks a defined hydrophobic core typical for globular domains.
source: The TCP domain structure lacks a defined hydrophobic core typical for globular domains, and both sides of its β-sheet are exposed to the solvent and well hydrated.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Both sides of the TCP domain β-sheet are exposed to the solvent and well hydrated.
source: The TCP domain structure lacks a defined hydrophobic core typical for globular domains, and both sides of its β-sheet are exposed to the solvent and well hydrated.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The overall sequence identity of the CPAP and STIL proteins between Drosophila and zebrafish is relatively low (approximately 22% and approximately 13%, respectively).
source: Although the overall sequence identity of the CPAP and STIL proteins between Drosophila and zebrafish is relatively low (∼22% and ∼13%, respectively), our structural analysis revealed that the interaction interface is conserved, confirming the previous proposal that fly Ana2 is the functional homologue of vertebrate STIL (Stevens et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is determined by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The interaction interface between CPAP and STIL is conserved between Drosophila and zebrafish.
source: Although the overall sequence identity of the CPAP and STIL proteins between Drosophila and zebrafish is relatively low (∼22% and ∼13%, respectively), our structural analysis revealed that the interaction interface is conserved, confirming the previous proposal that fly Ana2 is the functional homologue of vertebrate STIL (Stevens et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison of the complexes from both species.

claim: Fly Ana2 is the functional homologue of vertebrate STIL.
source: Although the overall sequence identity of the CPAP and STIL proteins between Drosophila and zebrafish is relatively low (∼22% and ∼13%, respectively), our structural analysis revealed that the interaction interface is conserved, confirming the previous proposal that fly Ana2 is the functional homologue of vertebrate STIL (Stevens et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is confirmed by structural conservation and supported by prior literature.

claim: There is a remarkable correlation between the ability of mutant proteins to bind to one another in vitro and their ability to support centriole assembly in vivo.
source: Our mutational analysis of the interface demonstrates a remarkable correlation between the ability of mutant proteins to bind to one another in vitro and their ability to support centriole assembly in vivo, providing compelling support for our structural model of the metazoan CPAP–STIL complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ITC binding data with functional rescue data.

claim: E1235 in human CPAP is one of several residues involved in the binding interface with STIL, making an important sidechain–mainchain contact.
source: The structures we report here reveal that E1235 is one of the several residues involved in the binding interface with STIL, making an important sidechain–mainchain contact.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and inferred from the zebrafish structure.

claim: The E1235V mutation can compromise complex formation between CPAP and STIL.
source: This structural model explains how the E1235V mutation can compromise complex formation, and we have confirmed that this is the case with zebrafish proteins in vitro.
evidence: This is confirmed by ITC experiments with the equivalent mutation in zebrafish.

claim: The equivalent E792V mutation in fly dCPAP leads to inefficient centriole assembly, but this process is not abolished.
source: Moreover, the equivalent mutation in flies leads to inefficient centriole assembly, but this process is not abolished.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in Drosophila showing intermediate phenotype.

claim: It is a partial failure in centriole assembly that is the primary cause of microcephaly in patients with the E1235V mutation.
source: Taken together, our data strongly suggest that it is a partial failure in centriole assembly that is the primary cause of microcephaly in these patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data showing partial loss of function.
